title: The Impact of Using Spherical Video-Based Virtual Reality and Conventional Video on Writing Competence, Motivation, Class Engagement, and Learning Perception
venue: International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether spherical video-based virtual reality (SVVR) improves students’ observational writing more than conventional video, while also exploring effects on writing motivation, classroom engagement, and student perceptions. The core problem motivating the study is that students often struggle to generate ideas and produce detailed observational texts when instruction relies on traditional methods that do not provide immersive or concrete experiences.

The intervention compared two forms of media-supported writing instruction: SVVR for the experimental group and conventional video for the control group. Both groups received instruction on observational text writing and then observed the same kinds of objects (e.g., natural conditions, human and animal body structures, and buildings), but through different media. The SVVR condition used immersive 360-degree spherical video delivered through a head-worn device, while the control condition viewed equivalent content in standard MP4 video format. Quantitative measures included a researcher-developed observational writing rubric, a writing motivation scale, and a classroom engagement questionnaire; qualitative data came from semi-structured interviews.

The study involved 250 junior high school students aged 13–15 in Indonesia, apparently at a single junior high school site acknowledged as Cendrawasih Junior High School in South Tangerang. The intervention lasted one semester (six months). Although the paper labels the design quasi-experimental, it also includes qualitative interviews and reports that participants were randomly assigned to experimental and control groups; however, the overall methodological profile is best characterized as mixed-methods because it combines quantitative comparison and thematic interview analysis.

The authors conclude that SVVR was more effective than conventional video for improving observational writing, especially in organization and content, and also increased writing motivation, classroom engagement, and positive perceptions of learning. Students reported that immersive features such as 360-degree viewing, video, background sound, and quizzes helped them observe more closely and write more concretely. The paper frames these gains as resulting from richer situational experience and more engaging instruction, though all outcomes were measured immediately after the intervention with no delayed follow-up.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed K-12 quasi-experimental comparison study with a sizeable sample (n=250), pre/post measures, and multiple quantitative analyses, but it is not a clear randomized controlled trial and the reporting contains substantial table inconsistencies and unclear statistics that weaken credibility.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive effects of SVVR on writing and engagement, including a large within-group pre-post effect for writing (r=0.83), but inconsistent statistical reporting and unclear between-group estimates make the magnitude somewhat uncertain rather than firmly blue-tier.

interventions.use_case: Spherical video-based virtual reality used to provide immersive 360° observation experiences before students write junior-high observational texts about natural conditions, body structures, and buildings.
Conventional video-based writing instruction used as the comparison condition, presenting the same observational content in MP4/video-projector format before writing.

finding.finding_summary: The quasi-experimental study reported that students in the spherical video-based virtual reality condition outperformed the conventional video group on observational writing competence after a 6-month intervention. Within-group improvement was reported for the SVVR group from pretest to posttest (z=-2.54, p=0.04, r=0.83), while the control group showed no significant pre-post gain (z=-1.93, p=0.08, r=0.70); between-group analyses also favored SVVR on organization (U=786, p=.042) and content (U=710, p=.004), with no significant differences on feeling or vocabulary dimensions.
finding.measure: Observational writing competence rubric assessing organization, content, emotional expression, and vocabulary use; A/B rubric levels plus pre/post writing scores
finding.effect_size: r=0.83 (SVVR pre-post); r=0.70 (control pre-post); other between-group effect sizes not_reported
finding.std_deviation: Pre/post SDs reported unclearly in text/tables; exact usable SDs not_reported

finding.finding_summary: SVVR was reported to improve writing motivation and classroom engagement relative to conventional video. For motivation, descriptive gains favored the experimental group across interest, importance, emotion, and expectation, although the reported independent-samples t-test table contains inconsistencies and mostly non-significant p-values; for engagement, ANCOVA results favored SVVR overall (F=0.687, p=0.032, eta2=0.008) and on behavioral (F=4.583, p=0.022, eta2=0.009), cognitive (F=6.328, p=0.044, eta2=0.052), and emotional engagement (F=5.267, p=0.028, eta2=0.003).
finding.measure: Writing motivation Likert scale; classroom engagement questionnaire covering behavioral/affective-cognitive/emotional engagement
finding.effect_size: eta2=0.008 overall engagement; eta2=0.009 behavioral; eta2=0.052 cognitive; eta2=0.003 emotional
finding.std_deviation: Engagement SDs reported: experimental 0.47 overall, 0.42 behavioral, 0.47 cognitive, 0.63 emotional; control 0.63 overall, 0.50 behavioral, 0.58 cognitive, 0.69 emotional

finding.finding_summary: The conventional video comparison condition showed smaller and statistically non-significant within-group improvement on writing competence from pretest to posttest. Reported results for the control group were z=-1.93, p=0.08, r=0.70, and the group was generally outperformed by SVVR on overall rubric classifications and on organization/content dimensions.
finding.measure: Observational writing competence rubric assessing organization, content, emotional expression, and vocabulary use
finding.effect_size: r=0.70 (control pre-post); between-group effect sizes not_reported
